title: Did an Apple Hit Newton on the Head? In 1726, He Himself Said It Only Fell
description:
An apple hits Newton's head; he conceives universal gravitation: told for nearly 300 years. Yet on April 15, 1726, at tea with Dr. Stukeley under apple trees in Kensington, Newton, 83, said only "an apple fell." Stukeley's 1752 memoir (printed only in 1936): no place, no year, no hit on the head. Voltaire (1727) and Conduitt's drafts: it just falls (his years 1665/1666 clash); Newton's late notes: in 1666 he began thinking of gravity reaching the Moon; no apple. The earliest "hit his head" so far: an anonymous pamphlet's 2nd edition, c. 1740 (not in the 1739 1st), citing Pemberton, whose 1728 book has only garden and Moon. Euler (1760) says so too; the first big Newton biography (1831) omitted the apple: no source. Woolsthorpe's tree was shown to visitors by 1806; blown down c. 200 years ago, it re-rooted and still bears fruit.

Limits: the niece line came only in Voltaire's 1741 new edition; "hit his head" is only the earliest found so far; Stukeley's diary and the 1912 letter come via researchers; the tree's fall year is disputed, so not given; no evidence Newton picked this tree. Sources below.

AI-generated art; historical figures are unnamed cartoons, not likenesses; no modern researchers drawn.

Data as of 2026-10-20 (rewritten 2026-10-25, new rules)

chapters.doctor-name: 1752: the doctor puts that afternoon in a manuscript
chapters.london-book: 1727, the year Newton died: a book in London
chapters.conduitt-mint: The Mint deputy's biography drafts: the years clash
chapters.pamphlet: Around 1740: a pamphlet's 2nd edition adds a passage

nw001.text: You've heard it: an apple hit Newton's head; he thought of gravity.

nw002.text: That knock went from storybooks to textbooks; yet the record nearest Newton sat 184 years unprinted.

nw003.text: April 15, 1726, London. A doctor is having tea with Newton, 83, under the apple trees.

nw004.text: Newton said it was just like this when gravity first came to mind: an apple fell.

nw005.text: Oddly, the doctor's diary that day records the visit, but no apple.

nw006.text: Odder still: over a decade after his death, a pamphlet's reprint added a passage.

nw007.text: One night about 200 years ago, a gale blew toward his old home's apple tree.

nw008.text: This file follows that apple from that cup of tea to today's tree: 300 years.

nw009.text: Did that apple really hit his head?

nw101.text: Whether it did, the other man there that day knew best: the doctor, Stukeley.

nw102.text: The apple isn't in his diary; it's in a memoir manuscript he finished in 1752.

nw118.text: Today the manuscript is held by Britain's Royal Society.

nw103.text: The manuscript details Newton's words: that time, he was sitting in thought.

nw104.text: He thought: why should an apple always fall straight down to the ground?

nw105.text: Why not sideways, or upward, but always toward the Earth's center?

nw106.text: His answer: the Earth pulls it; in matter there must be a pulling power, proportional to its quantity;

nw107.text: So the apple pulls the Earth, too.

nw108.text: This is the closest record found to Newton's own account; even so, it's Stukeley's retelling.

nw109.text: Where did the apple fall? What year? Did it touch him?

nw110.text: The manuscript has none of the three: no place, no year, just "formerly";

nw111.text: nor a single word saying the apple hit his head.

nw112.text: Replay Newton's words: he said it "fell." The first time I read this, I did a double take too.

nw113.text: In the whole manuscript, the apple is only here.

nw114.text: So who dug out the diary from the start, the one with no apple?

nw115.text: A scholar who studies Newton's apple tree. The entry that day: April 15, dined alone with Newton at his Kensington lodgings.

nw116.text: Remember the 184 years from the start?

nw119.text: Written in 1752, the manuscript was printed as a book only in 1936; only that year did it reach the Royal Society.

nw117.text: But was Stukeley the only one who wrote this apple down?

nw201.text: No. In March 1727, Newton died; that same year, a book in English came out in London, mentioning the apple.

nw202.text: Its author: the French writer Voltaire, in England when Newton died.

nw203.text: He wrote: walking in his garden, Newton saw an apple fall from a tree and had his first idea of a theory of gravity.

nw204.text: This time he's walking, not sitting; I only noticed on my second read.

nw205.text: And who did Voltaire hear it from?

nw206.text: Not in this book. Over a decade later, in 1741, in a new edition of another book, he added a line:

nw208.text: That passage: one day in the country, Newton saw fruit fall from a tree and got lost in thought:

nw209.text: What makes everything fall in a direction nearly toward the Earth's center?

nw210.text: This niece kept house for Newton; notice, she said "fruit," not even naming an apple.

nw211.text: Who else near Newton left a record?

nw301.text: The niece's husband, Conduitt, was Newton's deputy at the Mint.

nw302.text: After Newton died, Conduitt began a biography of him, leaving several drafts.

nw303.text: The drafts say plague shut Cambridge; Newton went home to Lincolnshire;

nw321.text: He was 23 or 24, and stayed in the country nearly two years in all.

nw304.text: One draft has him musing in a garden on the power that makes apples fall;

nw320.text: another has him see an apple fall from a tree.

nw306.text: The same man's drafts say 1665 in some, 1666 in others.

nw307.text: Picture writing a late elder's life from hearsay: you'd likely get years like this too.

nw308.text: Whichever year, none of these writers says it hit his head.

nw309.text: Notice? Each time it changes hands, Newton changes posture: sitting, walking. A third is coming soon.

nw310.text: And Newton himself? Of all his manuscripts, did he ever write this down?

nw311.text: In a late note, Newton listed one by one what he had worked out when young:

nw312.text: series, tangents, then the colors of light;

nw313.text: Reaching 1666, he says: that year, I began to wonder whether gravity could reach all the way to the Moon.

nw314.text: Between the lines he added: all this was in the two plague years.

nw316.text: The whole note has the Moon, no apple; to date, no apple in Newton's own hand has been found.

nw317.text: That's odd: think about it, the man best placed to tell of this apple, writing on gravity himself, noted only the Moon.

nw318.text: So where's the earliest "hit his head" found so far?

nw401.text: In the pamphlet reprint from the start, printed around 1740.

nw402.text: Its first edition, published in London in 1739, never once mentions Newton; its author is still unknown.

nw403.text: The result? The second edition adds a passage:

nw404.text: As Newton sat under a tree, an apple fell on his head: the hint for his gravity theory.

nw405.text: The author adds: but he had to be a mathematician;

nw406.text: otherwise, if a whole orchard's fruit fell on him, he'd only find it heavy and hard.

nw407.text: That line truly made me laugh. Notice: here, at last, the apple touches his head.

nw408.text: It cites whom as its source?

nw409.text: The book says: according to Pemberton.

nw410.text: Pemberton edited the Principia's 3rd edition; he asked Newton how the theory arose.

nw411.text: Does Pemberton's own book have this apple?

nw412.text: In 1728, Pemberton published a book on Newton's ideas; its preface says Newton, sitting alone in a garden, mused on gravity:

nw413.text: Why not as high as the Moon? he said to himself.

nw414.text: A garden and the Moon, but no apple; the source the pamphlet cites doesn't have it.

nw415.text: Say you cite a book, and the line isn't in it; today, the comment section would probably call that out.

nw416.text: Does the head version appear only in this pamphlet?

nw501.text: There's a letter too. In September 1760, mathematician Euler wrote to a German princess, also about Newton.

nw502.text: It says that one day this great English philosopher and mathematician lay under a garden apple tree,

nw503.text: and an apple fell on his head.

nw505.text: Euler goes on: yet the Moon didn't fall on his head; so he thought its motion might be what keeps the Moon from falling.

nw506.text: He adds: if Newton hadn't lain under that tree, nor the apple fallen just on his head, we might still not know.

nw507.text: How far did this letter travel?

nw508.text: The letters became a book in 1768; the 1795 English translation also has the apple fall on his head.

nw509.text: But did everyone who read it believe it?

nw510.text: The editor of a late-1700s Paris edition noted here:

nw511.text: Newton saying he got it "by thinking on it continually" sounds truer than the apple.

nw512.text: Doubts aside, by the 19th century the head hit was the common version.

nw513.text: In 1829, a commentator joked about it:

nw522.text: Anyone else hit by an apple would likely eat it first, not ponder gravity.

nw514.text: Your childhood textbook's apple was likely this one.

nw515.text: Yet just then, one man didn't dare write it.

nw516.text: In 1831, the first big biography of Newton came out.

nw523.text: The author notes he found no source for the apple story, and dared not use it.

nw517.text: Over 20 years on, he reversed and put the apple back; the reason: Newton's niece told Voltaire.

nw518.text: I love this: a careful biographer sought a source even for the apple; the head hit was already everywhere.

nw519.text: An apple tree at Newton's home became "the one," too.

nw520.text: When was it first pointed out?

nw601.text: The earliest record so far: an 1806 local history says the apple tree stands, shown to visitors.

nw602.text: By then, Newton was nearly 80 years dead; the record came 60-odd years after the head-hit pamphlet.

nw603.text: Did Newton himself identify this tree?

nw604.text: No evidence. The scholar who studies the tree thinks it was picked because Newton's garden had only this apple tree.

nw605.text: In fact, one man saw that garden long before.

nw621.text: In 1721, Stukeley visited Newton's birthplace; the host took him up to Newton's study.

nw606.text: His record never mentions an apple tree; but that year, he hadn't heard the apple story yet.

nw620.text: The scholar who studies the tree quoted a 1912 letter.

nw608.text: The writer said his father, as a boy, heard the day after a gale that Newton's apple tree had fallen.

nw622.text: His teacher took the class to saw off limbs.

nw609.text: The fallen trunk took root again; today it still blooms and bears fruit at the manor.

nw610.text: If you visit, you'll see an old tree grown from a fallen trunk, ringed by a low fence.

nw611.text: So, the opening question: did that apple really hit Newton's head?

nw612.text: Whether the apple truly led him to gravity, the records can't settle it; honestly, even scholars split.

nw613.text: Some demote it to an unsupported anecdote;

nw623.text: the scholar who studies the tree says Newton would hardly risk his soul over so small a thing.

nw614.text: Other historians think, recalling events 60 years back, the aging Newton may have been building his legend.

nw615.text: Yet the head part can close: the apple's recorded; the head came later.

nw617.text: As a kid, did you hear the apple hit his head? Tell me.

nw618.text: This channel tells only what records hold. Subscribe to open files with us.
